title: (Scenario) The consumer app is running with no errors, but messages sit in the topic unconsumed — how do you diagnose it: (1) the consumer group ALREADY committed those offsets (Kafka doesn't redeliver — reset offsets or use a new group.id), (2) auto.offset.reset=latest on a brand-new group SKIPPED all pre-existing messages (set earliest if you need the backlog), (3) more consumers than partitions so some consumers are IDLE (a partition is owned by exactly one consumer per group), or (4) the group is stuck rebalancing — and which tools confirm it (kafka-consumer-groups --describe to see per-partition CURRENT-OFFSET/LOG-END-OFFSET/LAG and member assignment)?
shortTitle: (Scenario) The consumer app is running with no errors, but messages sit in the topic unconsumed — how do you diagnose it?

s1_definition.profdef: When a consumer runs cleanly but messages appear unconsumed, the cause is almost always about offsets, group membership, or partition assignment rather than a crash. The four classic causes are: the group already committed past those offsets so Kafka will not redeliver them, a brand-new group with `auto.offset.reset=latest` skipped all pre-existing messages, there are more consumers than partitions so some consumers are idle because a partition is owned by exactly one consumer per group, or the group is stuck rebalancing and not stably assigned. You diagnose with `kafka-consumer-groups --describe`, which shows each partition's current offset, log-end offset, lag, and which member owns it.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine transfer slips piling up in a tray at National Bank of India while the clerk insists they are working fine. Maybe the clerk already stamped those slips as done earlier, so they ignore them now. Maybe a new clerk was told to only handle slips arriving after they sat down, so the old pile is invisible to them. Maybe there are five clerks but only three trays, so two clerks sit idle with nothing assigned. Or maybe the team is in the middle of reshuffling who owns which tray and nobody is actually working yet. To find out, you check the official register that shows each tray's done-mark, its newest slip, the gap, and which clerk owns it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Unconsumed-but-no-errors is usually already-committed offsets, a latest reset skipping the backlog, more consumers than partitions leaving some idle, or a stuck rebalance, and consumer-groups describe shows the offsets, lag, and assignment that tell you which.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a consumer runs cleanly but messages appear unconsumed, the cause is almost always about offsets, group membership, or partition assignment rather than a crash. The four classic causes are: the group already committed past those offsets so Kafka will not redeliver them, a brand-new group with `auto.offset.reset=latest` skipped all pre-existing messages, there are more consumers than partitions so some consumers are idle because a partition is owned by exactly one consumer per group, or the group is stuck rebalancing and not stably assigned. You diagnose with `kafka-consumer-groups --describe`, which shows each partition's current offset, log-end offset, lag, and which member owns it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine transfer slips piling up in a tray at National Bank of India while the clerk insists they are working fine. Maybe the clerk already stamped those slips as done earlier, so they ignore them now. Maybe a new clerk was told to only handle slips arriving after they sat down, so the old pile is invisible to them. Maybe there are five clerks but only three trays, so two clerks sit idle with nothing assigned. Or maybe the team is in the middle of reshuffling who owns which tray and nobody is actually working yet. To find out, you check the official register that shows each tray's done-mark, its newest slip, the gap, and which clerk owns it.

**One line to remember:** Unconsumed-but-no-errors is usually already-committed offsets, a latest reset skipping the backlog, more consumers than partitions leaving some idle, or a stuck rebalance, and consumer-groups describe shows the offsets, lag, and assignment that tell you which.

sections.s2_technical:
The first cause is that the group already committed those offsets. Kafka does not redeliver committed messages to the same group, because the committed offset marks them as consumed. If someone ran the consumer earlier and it committed through the latest offset, then a fresh run of the same group sees nothing new to process even though the records still physically exist in the topic for their retention period. The fix is either to reset the group's offsets back, using `kafka-consumer-groups --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute`, or to use a new `group.id`, which has no committed offsets and therefore follows the reset policy.

The second cause is `auto.offset.reset=latest` on a brand-new group. For a group with no committed offset, latest starts at the end of each partition, so every record that already existed before the consumer joined is skipped silently. The app runs without errors and simply waits for new records, while the backlog sits untouched. The fix is to set `auto.offset.reset=earliest` if you need the backlog, then either restart the new group or reset its offsets to earliest.

The third cause is more consumers than partitions. Within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so if a topic has three partitions and you run five consumers in the group, two consumers get no partitions and sit idle doing nothing, which can look like messages are not being consumed if you are watching those idle instances. The data is still consumed by the three active consumers, but the idle ones mislead you. The fix is to match or exceed partitions to the parallelism you need, since you cannot have more active consumers in a group than partitions.

The fourth cause is a group stuck rebalancing. If members keep joining and leaving, perhaps because of a blown poll interval or flapping instances, the group spends its time rebalancing and never settles into stable assignment, so little or no processing happens. The describe command shows the group in a rebalancing or preparing state and may show no stable member assignment. The fix is to stabilize membership: fix the slow processing that trips the poll interval, stop the flapping, and let the group settle.

The diagnostic tool is `kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server ... --describe --group yourgroup`. It prints, per partition, the current offset the group has committed, the log-end offset which is the newest record, and the lag which is the difference. It also shows which consumer member and client host owns each partition. Reading this tells you the cause directly: if current offset equals log-end offset with zero lag, the group already consumed everything, pointing to cause one or two; if lag is high but no member owns the partitions, you have idle consumers or a rebalance problem; if some partitions have no owner, membership is unstable. A senior nuance is to also check the group state field, which shows Stable, PreparingRebalance, or CompletingRebalance, and to confirm the consumer is actually subscribed to the topic you think it is, since a topic name typo produces the same symptom.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India deploys a new reconciliation consumer, but operators report that transactions sit in the topic unconsumed while the app logs no errors. The on-call engineer must diagnose which of the four causes it is.

Problem 1 — maybe a previous run already committed those offsets, so Kafka will not redeliver them. The engineer must check committed offset versus log-end offset.

Problem 2 — maybe the new group used latest and skipped the backlog. The engineer must check whether lag equals the backlog and the reset policy.

Problem 3 — maybe there are more consumer instances than partitions, so some are idle. The engineer must check member assignment against partition count.

Problem 4 — maybe the group is stuck rebalancing. The engineer must check the group state.

The code will model a diagnostic helper that, given per-partition offsets, member assignments, and group state, reports the most likely cause and the fix, logged for the reconciliation group.

```bash
  --describe --group reconciliation

  --group reconciliation --reset-offsets --to-earliest --topic transactions --execute
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four snapshots of the reconciliation group, each representing one of the classic causes.

Step 1 — in case A the group is stable, lag is zero, and the current offset equals the log-end offset. The diagnoser concludes the group already committed everything, so Kafka will not redeliver, and the fix is to reset offsets or use a new group id.

Step 2 — in case B the group is stable, it is brand new, the reset policy is latest, and there is large lag with the current offset at zero. The diagnoser concludes latest skipped the backlog, so the fix is to set earliest and reset to earliest to read the pending records.

Step 3 — in case C the group is stable with five members but only three partitions. The diagnoser concludes two consumers are idle because a partition is owned by exactly one consumer per group, so the fix is to add partitions or remove consumers.

Step 4 — in case D the group state is preparing-rebalance, not stable. The diagnoser concludes the group is stuck rebalancing and processes nothing until membership stabilizes, so the fix is to stop the churn, often by fixing slow processing that trips the poll interval.

```
2026-10-24 23:30:01 [INFO] Case A → ALREADY COMMITTED (current==log-end, lag 0) → reset offsets or use a new group.id; Kafka does not redeliver
2026-10-24 23:30:01 [INFO] Case B → LATEST SKIPPED BACKLOG → set auto.offset.reset=earliest and reset to earliest to read the 5000 pending records
2026-10-24 23:30:01 [INFO] Case C → MORE CONSUMERS THAN PARTITIONS (5>3) → 2 idle; add partitions or remove consumers
2026-10-24 23:30:01 [INFO] Case D → STUCK REBALANCING (state=PreparingRebalance) → stabilize membership (fix slow processing / flapping)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Symptom: messages sit unconsumed, app logs no errors
    │
    ▼
  Run: kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group reconciliation
    │  reads CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET, LAG, MEMBER, STATE
    ▼
  Decision tree:
    ├─ state != Stable ──────────────→ STUCK REBALANCING (stabilize members)
    ├─ lag == 0 & current == log-end ─→ ALREADY COMMITTED (reset / new group.id)
    ├─ new group & reset=latest & lag>0→ LATEST SKIPPED BACKLOG (set earliest)
    ├─ members > partitions ──────────→ IDLE CONSUMERS (add partitions / fewer)
    └─ else ──────────────────────────→ healthy, backlog draining

  Fix applied → re-run --describe → lag decreasing → resolved
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a consumer runs cleanly but messages sit unconsumed, I look at offsets, membership, and assignment, not at a crash, because there is no error. There are four classic causes. The first is that the group already committed those offsets, and Kafka does not redeliver committed messages to the same group, so the records exist physically but the group has nothing new to read. The fix is to reset the group's offsets backward or use a brand-new group id.

The second cause is a brand-new group with the reset policy set to latest, which starts at the end of each partition and silently skips everything that already existed. The app waits for new records while the backlog is untouched, so the fix is to set the policy to earliest and reset to earliest if you need that backlog. The third cause is running more consumers than partitions, because within a group a partition is owned by exactly one consumer, so extra consumers sit idle and can mislead you into thinking nothing is consumed, when really the active consumers handle all partitions. The fix is to add partitions or reduce consumers. The fourth cause is a group stuck rebalancing, often from a blown poll interval or flapping instances, where the group never settles into stable assignment and processes little.

The tool that tells me which cause it is is the consumer-groups describe command. It prints, per partition, the current committed offset, the log-end offset which is the newest record, the lag between them, and which member owns the partition, plus the group state. If lag is zero and current equals log-end, the group already consumed everything. If lag is high but no member owns the partitions, I have idle consumers or an unstable group. The group state field distinguishes a stable group from one stuck preparing a rebalance.

In my National Bank of India work, a new reconciliation consumer once appeared to process nothing with no errors. The describe output showed large lag with the current offset at zero and the reset policy set to latest on a fresh group, so it had skipped the whole backlog. We changed the policy to earliest and reset the offsets to earliest, and the backlog drained immediately. Having that decision tree and that one command turned a confusing non-error into a two-minute diagnosis.

---

keyPoints: auto.offset.reset: earliest (start from beginning) or latest (new only)
enable.auto.commit: false for manual control — commit after processing
max.poll.records: control batch size per poll
Consumer lag: difference between latest offset and committed offset
